name: Trough of Disillusionment
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Where the Real Technology Survives the Fake Enthusiasm
lesson.summary: The hype cycle's sobering third act, when failed pilots and cooling press attention separate technologies with real underlying value from those that never had a viable path.
lesson.body:
The Trough of Disillusionment is the hype cycle's third stage: public interest wanes, implementations that were launched during the peak fail to deliver, press coverage turns negative or simply moves on to the next Innovation Trigger, funding tightens sharply, and some producers fail or pivot away entirely.

This is not the technology getting worse. It is public sentiment correcting for the overshoot built up at the peak. Pilots launched during the peak, often undertaken for publicity or fear of missing out rather than a well scoped use case, report back with disappointing results, cost overruns, or outright failure to ship. Those failures are simply more newsworthy at this stage than the successes were during the climb, because the emperor has no clothes is now the more compelling story than the emperor's new clothes ever was.

The AI winters are a real and instructive example. Following the optimism around expert systems and DARPA funded programs like the Strategic Computing Initiative through the 1980s, commercial expert systems companies struggled to deliver on their promises, funding collapsed, and for a stretch of years in the late 1980s and early 1990s the term artificial intelligence itself became something investors and researchers were cautious about using. AI did eventually recover, which is a story for the Slope of Enlightenment beyond this chapter, but the trough was genuinely painful and lasted years.

The trough is where real progress often continues, just without much of an audience. The people still working on a technology during this stage are disproportionately practitioners motivated by the underlying problem rather than the publicity, and they tend to spend the quiet years fixing exactly the engineering problems that the peak era pilots exposed. This is why the trough functions as a filter rather than a graveyard: it separates ideas with genuine underlying value, which eventually climb the Slope of Enlightenment, from technologies that never had a viable path and simply fade from view.

It would be a mistake to assume every quiet period ends in recovery. The Segway is a fair example of a technology that generated enormous inflated expectations coverage around its 2001 launch, sold well below its projected volumes for years afterward, and never really climbed back to anything like a mass market plateau. The trough label is diagnostic in hindsight. On its own it is not a promise that recovery is coming.

Some analysts, including Gartner's own quantum computing hype cycle reports in recent years, have described the field as moving through trough like territory, as early enterprise pilots report modest or inconclusive results relative to how they were framed at launch. Treat that read as directional rather than precise, since exact positioning varies by edition and by which specific approach, superconducting, trapped ion, annealing, or photonic, is being assessed. Whether the field's current period ends in a genuine slope of enlightenment or a permanent, narrow plateau is exactly the kind of question this book keeps returning to rather than answering by assertion.
